claim: Intracerebral EEG data were collected in 30 subjects while they performed interleaved quiz and choice tasks.
source: Intracerebral EEG data were collected in a large group of subjects (n=30) while they were performing interleaved quiz and choice tasks that were designed to examine how a series of unrelated feedbacks affect decisions between safe and risky options.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of subjects and the tasks performed during data collection.

claim: Elevated broadband gamma activity (BGA) in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) signals periods of high mood.
source: Results showed that (1) elevated broadband gamma activity (BGA) in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and dorsal anterior insula (daIns) was respectively signaling periods of high and low mood
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study's results.

claim: Elevated broadband gamma activity (BGA) in the dorsal anterior insula (daIns) signals periods of low mood.
source: Results showed that (1) elevated broadband gamma activity (BGA) in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and dorsal anterior insula (daIns) was respectively signaling periods of high and low mood
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study's results.

claim: Increased vmPFC BGA promotes risk taking by overweighting gain prospects.
source: Results showed that (1) elevated broadband gamma activity (BGA) in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and dorsal anterior insula (daIns) was respectively signaling periods of high and low mood, (2) increased vmPFC and daIns BGA respectively promoted and tempered risk taking by overweighting gain vs. loss prospects.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study's results.

claim: Increased daIns BGA tempers risk taking by overweighting loss prospects.
source: Results showed that (1) elevated broadband gamma activity (BGA) in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and dorsal anterior insula (daIns) was respectively signaling periods of high and low mood, (2) increased vmPFC and daIns BGA respectively promoted and tempered risk taking by overweighting gain vs. loss prospects.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study's results.

claim: Incidental feedbacks induce brain states that correspond to different moods and bias the evaluation of risky options.
source: Thus, incidental feedbacks induce brain states that correspond to different moods and bias the evaluation of risky options.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion from the study.

claim: People experiencing positive outcome in some part of their life tend to expect success in any other.
source: More generally, these findings might explain why people experiencing positive (or negative) outcome in some part of their life tend to expect success (or failure) in any other.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a general implication of the findings.

claim: People experiencing negative outcome in some part of their life tend to expect failure in any other.
source: More generally, these findings might explain why people experiencing positive (or negative) outcome in some part of their life tend to expect success (or failure) in any other.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a general implication of the findings.

claim: Humans often make inconsistent decisions, even when facing seemingly identical choices.
source: Humans often make inconsistent decisions, even when facing seemingly identical choices.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as a known phenomenon.

claim: Brain activity preceding the presentation of choice options might provide a bias on the eventual choice, particularly when alternatives are safe vs. risky options.
source: In neuroscience, many studies have shown that brain activity preceding the presentation of choice options might provide a bias on the eventual choice, particularly when alternatives are safe vs. risky options (Chew et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2014; Kuhnen and Knutson, 2005; Lopez-Persem et al., 2016; Padoa-Schioppa, 2013; Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: Baseline brain activity could be related to mental constructs such as pleasantness, satiety, or mood, which were themselves under the influence of external events.
source: In some cases, baseline brain activity could be related to mental constructs such as pleasantness, satiety, or mood, which were themselves under the influence of external events (Abitbol et al., 2015; Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Good mood would lead to overweighting gain prospects and bad mood to overweighting loss prospects.
source: More precisely, good mood would lead to overweighting gain prospects and bad mood to overweighting loss prospects, making the overall expected value of a risky option positive or negative, depending on circumstances.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Mood has a well-documented impact on buying lottery tickets or investing in financial markets.
source: Such a mechanism could account for the well-documented impact of mood on buying lottery tickets or investing in financial markets (Bassi et al., 2013; Otto et al., 2016; Saunders, 1993), an effect that has been reproduced in the lab (Arkes et al., 1988; Chou et al., 2007; Eldar and Niv, 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies documenting this impact.

claim: Depressed and manic patients have opposite attitudes toward risk, respectively, focusing on negative and positive outcomes of potential actions.
source: It could also account for why depressed and manic patients have opposite attitudes toward risk, respectively, focusing on negative and positive outcomes of potential actions (Leahy, 1999; Yuen and Lee, 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting this claim about psychiatric patients.

claim: The underlying mechanism at the neural level of mood's impact on risky choice is still poorly understood.
source: Despite the importance of this phenomenon, producing disastrous decisions at both the individual scale in psychiatric conditions and the societal scale in real-life economics, the underlying mechanism at the neural level is still poorly understood.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this knowledge gap.

claim: Functional MRI has been mostly used to study mood fluctuations because mood fluctuations are difficult to track in animals, while invasive techniques are forbidden in humans for ethical reasons.
source: This is due to the limitations of functional MRI (fMRI), which has been mostly used because mood fluctuations are difficult to track in animals, while invasive techniques are forbidden in humans for obvious ethical reasons.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the reasons for fMRI predominance in this research area.

claim: Patients with refractory epilepsy implanted with deep electrodes prior to surgery offer the opportunity to record intracerebral EEG (iEEG) activity.
source: There is nonetheless a particular clinical situation that offers the opportunity to record intracerebral EEG (iEEG) activity from deep electrodes, when patients with refractory epilepsy are implanted prior to surgery.
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes this clinical opportunity.

claim: iEEG recordings have been used to successfully decode mood from resting-state activity.
source: These iEEG recordings have already been used to successfully decode mood from resting-state activity, a technical achievement that may open the route to closed-loop stimulation procedures (Bijanzadeh et al., 2013; Sani et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites studies that have used iEEG for mood decoding.

claim: iEEG recordings have been used to specify the impact of lateral orbitofrontal cortex stimulation aiming at improving mood in moderately depressed patients.
source: They have also been used to specify the impact of lateral orbitofrontal cortex stimulation aiming at improving mood in moderately depressed patients (Rao et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study that used iEEG for this purpose.

claim: Pioneering iEEG studies reported that changes in mood states might correspond to changes in the frequency of oscillatory activity.
source: There is however a discrepancy between these pioneering iEEG studies, which reported that changes in mood states might correspond to changes in the frequency of oscillatory activity (Bijanzadeh et al., 2013; Kirkby et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2018), and fMRI studies that have related mood fluctuations to the relative activity of opponent brain systems associated to either reward or punishment processing (Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites studies reporting this finding.

claim: fMRI studies have related mood fluctuations to the relative activity of opponent brain systems associated to either reward or punishment processing.
source: There is however a discrepancy between these pioneering iEEG studies, which reported that changes in mood states might correspond to changes in the frequency of oscillatory activity (Bijanzadeh et al., 2013; Kirkby et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2018), and fMRI studies that have related mood fluctuations to the relative activity of opponent brain systems associated to either reward or punishment processing (Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study reporting this finding.

claim: The study recorded iEEG activity while patients performed a task similar to that used in a previous fMRI study to induce mood fluctuations and test their impact on risky choices.
source: To examine whether good and bad mood are associated to activity in different brain regions or different frequency bands, we recorded iEEG activity while patients were performing a task similar to that used in a previous fMRI study to induce mood fluctuations and test their impact on risky choices (Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the study design.

claim: Mood fluctuations were induced by feedbacks provided to subjects on their responses to general knowledge questions.
source: Mood fluctuations were induced by feedbacks provided to subjects on their responses to general knowledge questions.
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the mood induction procedure.

claim: Choices were about whether to accept a challenge rewarded with monetary gains in case of success but punished with monetary losses in case of failure.
source: Choices were about whether to accept a challenge rewarded with monetary gains in case of success but punished with monetary losses in case of failure.
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the choice task.

claim: A computational model was developed to generate mood level as an integration of past feedbacks, the perception of which was itself modulated by mood level.
source: To avoid repeating self-report too frequently, a computational model was developed, building on previous suggestion (Eldar and Niv, 2015), to generate mood level as an integration of past feedbacks, the perception of which was itself modulated by mood level.
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the computational model development.

claim: Theoretical mood level (TML) was positively correlated with activity in brain regions classically associated with reward, such as the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).
source: This theoretical mood level (TML) was positively correlated with activity in brain regions classically associated with reward, such as the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), and negatively correlated with regions associated with punishment, such as the anterior insula (aIns).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this finding.

claim: Theoretical mood level (TML) was negatively correlated with regions associated with punishment, such as the anterior insula (aIns).
source: This theoretical mood level (TML) was positively correlated with activity in brain regions classically associated with reward, such as the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), and negatively correlated with regions associated with punishment, such as the anterior insula (aIns).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this finding.

claim: High vmPFC activity favored the risky option (accepting the challenge) by increasing the weight on potential gain.
source: Indeed, high vmPFC activity favored the risky option (accepting the challenge) by increasing the weight on potential gain, whereas high aIns activity favored the safe option (declining the challenge) by increasing the weight on potential loss.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this finding.

claim: High aIns activity favored the safe option (declining the challenge) by increasing the weight on potential loss.
source: Indeed, high vmPFC activity favored the risky option (accepting the challenge) by increasing the weight on potential gain, whereas high aIns activity favored the safe option (declining the challenge) by increasing the weight on potential loss.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this finding.

claim: The study intended to separate brain activity related to feedback events, to the overall mood level, and to the choice process.
source: Here, leveraging the excellent temporal resolution of iEEG, we intended to separate brain activity related to feedback events, to the overall mood level, and to the choice process.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this study objective.

claim: The study collected iEEG data in 30 patients suffering from refractory epilepsy (39.5±1.9 years old, 14 females).
source: iEEG data were collected in 30 patients suffering from refractory epilepsy (39.5±1.9 years old, 14 females, see demographic details in Table S1 in Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the patient demographics.

claim: In the quiz task, subjects were asked to answer general knowledge questions and received feedback on their response (correct, incorrect, or too late).
source: In the quiz task, subjects were asked to answer general knowledge questions and received feedback on their response (correct, incorrect, or too late).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the quiz task.

claim: The difficulty of questions and the validity of feedbacks were manipulated, unbeknownst to the subjects, so as to create episodes of high and low correct feedback rate.
source: In order to predictably modulate mood, the difficulty of questions and the validity of feedbacks were manipulated, unbeknownst to the subjects, so as to create episodes of high and low correct feedback rate (see Materials and methods, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the manipulation.

claim: In 25% of the trials, the effect of feedback history was assessed by asking subjects to rate their mood on a visual analog scale.
source: In 25% of the trials, the effect of feedback history was assessed by asking subjects to rate their mood on a visual analog scale.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the frequency of mood ratings.

claim: In 75% of trials, the quiz and choice task were separated by a 4-s rest period (black screen).
source: Otherwise (in 75% of trials), the quiz and choice task were separated by a 4-s rest period (black screen).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the rest period frequency.

claim: In the choice task, subjects had to decide whether to accept or reject a given offer before performing a challenge consisting in stopping a moving ball inside a target.
source: In the choice task, subjects had to decide whether to accept or reject a given offer before performing a challenge consisting in stopping a moving ball inside a target.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the choice task.

claim: The offer comprised a gain prospect (i.e. the amount of money they would win in case of success), a loss prospect (i.e. the amount of loss in case of failure), and the difficulty of the upcoming challenge (target size).
source: The offer comprised a gain prospect (i.e. the amount of money they would win in case of success), a loss prospect (i.e. the amount of loss in case of failure), and the difficulty of the upcoming challenge (target size).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the offer components.

claim: All three choice dimensions (gain, loss, and difficulty) were varied on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: All three choice dimensions (gain, loss, and difficulty) were varied on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the variation of choice dimensions.

claim: No feedback was provided regarding performance in the challenge to avoid learning and additional effects on mood.
source: In order to avoid learning and additional effects on mood, no feedback was provided regarding performance in the challenge (actual success rate was around 30% on average but significantly varied with difficulty).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the absence of feedback and the reason.

claim: Subjects were explicitly informed that the tasks were independent, such that responses to the quiz or mood ratings had no influence on choice options and hence on their monetary earnings.
source: Subjects were explicitly informed that the tasks were independent, such that responses to the quiz or mood ratings had no influence on choice options and hence on their monetary earnings.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the instructions given to subjects.

claim: Acceptance rate significantly increased with gain (βgain = 0.12 ± 0.02, t[29] = 6.85, and p=2.10–7).
source: Results show that acceptance rate significantly increased with gain (βgain = 0.12 ± 0.02, t[29] = 6.85, and p=2.10–7)
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: Acceptance rate significantly decreased with loss (βloss = –0.10 ± 0.02, t[29] = –5.51, and p=6.10–6).
source: but significantly decreased with loss (βloss = –0.10 ± 0.02, t[29] = –5.51, and p=6.10–6)
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: Acceptance rate significantly decreased with difficulty (βdiff = –0.03 ± 0.01, t[29] = –2.97, and p=6.10–3).
source: and difficulty (βdiff = –0.03 ± 0.01, t[29] = –2.97, and p=6.10–3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: There is a significantly positive association between mood ratings and choice residuals (β = 0.05 ± 0.02, t[29] = 2.32, and p=0.027).
source: Results indicate a significantly positive association between mood ratings and choice residuals (β = 0.05 ± 0.02, t[29] = 2.32, and p=0.027,)
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: Variability in choices, beyond that induced by the three dimensions of the offer, was partially explained by mood fluctuations.
source: meaning that variability in choices, beyond that induced by the three dimensions of the offer, was indeed partially explained by mood fluctuations.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this interpretation of the statistical finding.

claim: The proportion of correct feedbacks was higher in episodes with intended high vs. low correct feedback rate (0.60±0.01 vs. 0.21% ± 0.01%; t[29] = 22.99, p=4.10–20).
source: indeed the proportion of correct feedbacks was higher in episodes with intended high vs. low correct feedback rate (0.60±0.01 vs. 0.21% ± 0.01%; t[29] = 22.99, p=4.10–20; two-sided, paired Student's t-test)
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: Mood rating was higher in episodes with intended high vs. low correct feedback rate (0.22±0.04 to –0.12±0.06; t[29] = 3.76, p=8.10–4).
source: and so was mood rating (0.22±0.04 to –0.12±0.06; t[29] = 3.76, p=8.10–4, two-sided, paired, Student's t-test).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: The weight of mood on feedback (parameter δ) was significantly positive (t[29] = 3.30 and p=0.0026).
source: Conversely, the weight of mood on feedback (parameter δ) was also significantly positive (t[29] = 3.30 and p=0.0026).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding from the computational model.

claim: The forgetting factor was 0.69±0.04, meaning that feedback received five trials earlier still had an impact corresponding to 23% of the most recent feedback.
source: The forgetting factor was 0.69±0.04, meaning that feedback received five trials earlier still had an impact corresponding to 23% of the most recent feedback.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this parameter estimate and its interpretation.

claim: TML was significantly higher during episodes with high vs. low correct feedback rate (t[29] = 4.19 and p=2.10–4).
source: As seen with mood rating (Figure 1d), TML was significantly higher during episodes with high vs. low correct feedback rate (t[29] = 4.19 and p=2.10–4; two-sided, paired, Student's t-test).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: At the group level, Bayesian comparison indicated that the mood model was far more plausible (exceedance probability Xp = 1) than the null model assuming no influence of feedback but only the effect of time.
source: At the group level, Bayesian comparison indicated that the mood model was far more plausible (exceedance probability Xp = 1) than the null model assuming no influence of feedback but only the effect of time.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this Bayesian model comparison result.

claim: The null model did better than the mood model in 6 subjects (out of 30).
source: However, the results of model comparison were more variable at the individual level (see Figure 1d), with the null model doing better than the mood model in 6 subjects (out of 30).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this individual-level finding.

claim: The iEEG dataset included a total of 3494 recording sites (bipolar montage).
source: The iEEG dataset included a total of 3494 recording sites (bipolar montage, see Materials and methods) acquired from 30 patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the number of recording sites.

claim: Out of the 3494 recording sites, 3188 were free from artifacts and located within the gray matter of the 50 covered areas.
source: Out of the 3494 recording sites, 3188 were free from artifacts and located within the gray matter of the 50 covered areas.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the number of usable recording sites.

claim: Among the 50 covered areas, 42 regions (n=3154 sites) with at least 10 recording sites across at least 4 subjects were retained in the electrophysiological analyses.
source: Among these areas, 42 regions (n=3154 sites) with at least 10 recording sites across at least 4 subjects were retained in the electrophysiological analyses (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the selection criteria and number of retained regions.

claim: Broadband gamma activity (BGA) correlates positively with both fMRI and spiking activity.
source: We initially focused on broadband gamma activity (50–150 Hz, BGA), as converging lines of evidence showed that BGA correlates positively with both fMRI and spiking activity (Lachaux et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2009; Mukamel et al., 2005; Niessing et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007; Winawer et al., 2013)
evidence: The Results section cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: The vmPFC (n=91 sites from 20 subjects) was the only ROI for which a positive correlation was found between BGA and both mood rating and TML.
source: The vmPFC (n=91 sites from 20 subjects) was the only ROI for which we found a positive correlation (Figure 2b; Source data 1; Table S2 in Supplementary file 1) between BGA and both mood rating (best cluster: –1.37 to –1.04 s, sum[t(90)]=122.3, and pcorr=0.010) and TML (best cluster: –0.57 to –0.13 s, sum[t(90)]=132.4, and pcorr=8.10–3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this finding with statistical details.

claim: A negative correlation was found in the dorsal aIns (daIns) (n=86 sites from 28 subjects), in which BGA was negatively associated with both mood rating and TML.
source: Conversely, we found a negative correlation in a larger brain network encompassing the dorsal aIns (daIns) (n=86 sites from 28 subjects, Figure 2b; Source data 1; Table S2 in Supplementary file 1), in which BGA was negatively associated with both mood rating (best cluster: –3.36 to –2.51 s, sum[t(85)]=–325.8, and pcorr<1.7.10–5) and TML (best cluster: –3.13 to –2.72 s, sum[t(85)]=–136.4, and pcorr=9.10–3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this finding with statistical details.

claim: Additional brain regions in which BGA was negatively associated with mood level included the superior portion of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the lateral and rostro-mesial visual cortex, the ventral motor cortex, and the dorsomedial premotor cortex.
source: The additional brain regions in which BGA was negatively associated with mood level (indexed with either mood rating or TML) involved the superior portion of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the lateral and rostro-mesial visual cortex, the ventral motor cortex, and the dorsomedial premotor cortex (Table S2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly lists these additional regions.

claim: In the ventral aIns (vaIns), BGA was negatively associated with mood rating, but not with TML.
source: Note that in the ventral aIns (vaIns), BGA was negatively associated with mood rating, but not with TML.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this finding.

claim: The association between TML and BGA remained significant when only considering the 75% of trials with no rating (vmPFC: β=0.031 ± 9.10–3, t[90] = 3.59, and p=5.10–4; daIns: β=–0.02 ± 8.10–3, t[85] = –2.67, and p=9.10–3).
source: We also verified that the association between TML and BGA (averaged within the best temporal cluster for each ROI) remained significant when only considering the 75% of trials with no rating (vmPFC: β=0.031 ± 9.10–3, t[90] = 3.59, and p=5.10–4; daIns: β=–0.02 ± 8.10–3, t[85] = –2.67, and p=9.10–3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this verification with statistical details.

claim: BGA in the vmPFC and daIns carried non-redundant information about mood level.
source: Thus, BGA in the two main ROIs carried non-redundant information about mood level.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this conclusion based on the regression analysis.

claim: In the vmPFC, regression estimates were significantly positive for high-mood trials only (βhigh TML = 0.17 ± 0.08, t[90] = 2.10, and p=0.039), not for low-mood trials.
source: In the vmPFC, regression estimates were significantly positive for high-mood trials only (βhigh TML = 0.17 ± 0.08, t[90] = 2.10, and p=0.039; two-sided, one-sample, Student's t-test), not for low-mood trials.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: In the daIns, regression estimates only reached significance for low-mood trials (βlow TML = –0.14 ± 0.06, t[85] = –2.39, and p=0.019), not high-mood trials.
source: Conversely, in the daIns, regression estimates only reached significance for low-mood trials (βlow TML = –0.14 ± 0.06, t[85] = –2.39, and p=0.019), not high-mood trials.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: The vmPFC signals mood level when it gets better than average and the daIns when it gets worse than average.
source: This double dissociation suggests that the vmPFC signals mood level when it gets better than average and the daIns when it gets worse than average.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this interpretation of the double dissociation.

claim: BGA in the vmPFC was still a significant predictor of TML after removing the influence of the last feedback (β[–0.57, –0.13]=0.024 ± 8.10–3, t[90] = 2.99, and p=4.10–3).
source: BGA in the best time clusters identified above was still significant predictors of TML (after removing the influence of the last feedback) in both the vmPFC (β[–0.57, –0.13]=0.024 ± 8.10–3, t[90] = 2.99, and p=4.10–3)
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: BGA in the daIns was still a significant predictor of TML after removing the influence of the last feedback (β[–3.13, –2.72]=–0.021 ± 8.10–3, t[85] = –2.64, and p=0.010).
source: and daIns (β[–3.13, –2.72]=–0.021 ± 8.10–3, t[85] = –2.64, and p=0.010; two-sided, one-sample, Student's t-test).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: In the vmPFC, regression estimates were only significant in the high-gamma band (βHγ=0.091 ± 0.04, t[90] = 2.41, and p=0.018).
source: In the vmPFC, regression estimates were only significant in the high-gamma band (βHγ=0.091 ± 0.04, t[90] = 2.41, and p=0.018; two-sided, one-sample, Student's t-test).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: In the daIns, regression estimates were significantly negative in the gamma and high-gamma bands (βHγ=–0.067 ± 0.03, t[85] = –2.18, and p=0.032; βγ = –0.067 ± 0.03, t[85] = –2.0, and p=0.048).
source: In the daIns however, regression estimates were not only significantly negative in the gamma and high-gamma bands (βHγ=–0.067 ± 0.03, t[85] = –2.18, and p=0.032; βγ = –0.067 ± 0.03, t[85] = –2.0, and p=0.048)
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: In the daIns, regression estimates were significantly positive in the theta and beta bands (ββ=0.082 ± 0.04, t[85] = 2.31, and p=0.023; βθ=0.062 ± 0.02, t[85] = 2.85, and p=6.10–3).
source: but also significantly positive in the theta and beta bands (ββ=0.082 ± 0.04, t[85] = 2.31, and p=0.023; βθ=0.062 ± 0.02, t[85] = 2.85, and p=6.10–3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: In both vmPFC and daIns, Bayesian model selection designated the BGA-only GLM as providing the best account of TML (vmPFC: expected frequency Ef = 0.99 and exceedance probability Xp = 1; daIns: Ef = 0.99 and Xp = 1).
source: In both vmPFC and daIns, Bayesian model selection designated the BGA-only GLM as providing the best account of TML (vmPFC: expected frequency Ef = 0.99 and exceedance probability Xp = 1; daIns: Ef = 0.99 and Xp = 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this Bayesian model selection result.

claim: BGA was the best neural proxy for mood level, at least in the vmPFC and daIns.
source: Thus, even if other frequency band activity was significantly related to TML in daIns, it carried redundant information relative to that extracted from BGA. Hence, BGA was the best neural proxy for mood level, at least in our two main ROIs.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this conclusion based on the frequency band analysis.

claim: Brain regions showing a significant positive association between choice and BGA included the mid-cingulate, dorsal, rostral, and ventral medial prefrontal cortex, the vaIns, the rostral inferior temporal cortex, and parts of the visual and motor cortex.
source: The brain regions showing a significant positive association between choice and BGA included the mid-cingulate, dorsal, rostral, and ventral medial prefrontal cortex, the vaIns, the rostral inferior temporal cortex, and parts of the visual and motor cortex.
evidence: The Results section explicitly lists these regions.

claim: Negative association between choice and BGA was observed in regions such as the rostro-ventral premotor cortex, the posterior and daIns, and the ventral inferior and the superior parietal cortex.
source: Negative association between choice and BGA was observed in regions such as the rostro-ventral premotor cortex, the posterior and daIns, and the ventral inferior and the superior parietal cortex (Table S3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly lists these regions.

claim: Among regions that encoded mood levels in their baseline, regression estimates were significant in only two ROIs, namely a positive correlation in vmPFC and negative correlation in daIns.
source: Therefore, among regions that encoded mood levels in their baseline, regression estimates were significant in only two ROIs (Figure 3a; Source data 2), namely a positive correlation in vmPFC (best cluster: –1.64 to –1.31 s, sum[t(90)]=91.2, and pcorr=0.020) and negative correlation in daIns (best cluster: –0.95 to –0.67 s, sum[t(85)]=–85.2, and pcorr=0.029).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this finding with statistical details.

claim: vmPFC and daIns baseline BGA not only express mood in opposite fashion but also had opposite influence on upcoming choice.
source: Taken together, these results mean that vmPFC and daIns baseline BGA not only express mood in opposite fashion but also had opposite influence on upcoming choice.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: In the vmPFC, regression estimates were significantly positive for high-mood trials only (βhigh TML = 0.06 ± 0.01, t[90] = 5.64, and p=2.10–7), not for low-mood trials.
source: In the vmPFC, regression estimates were significantly positive for high-mood trials only (βhigh TML = 0.06 ± 0.01, t[90] = 5.64, and p=2.10–7; two-sided, one-sample, Student's t-test), not for low-mood trials.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: In the daIns, regression estimates only reached significance for low-mood trials (βlow TML = –0.05 ± 0.01, t[85] = –4.63, and p=1.10–5), not for high-mood trials.

source: This double dissociation suggests that the vmPFC positively predicts choice when mood gets better than average, and the daIns negatively predicts choice when mood gets worse than average.

source: For the vmPFC, we found that when baseline BGA was high, choice-related BGA positively predicted choices (best cluster: –1.41 to –1.16 s, sum[t(90)]=70.4, and pcorr=0.035).

claim: For the daIns, when baseline BGA was high, choice-related BGA negatively predicts choices (best cluster: –0.74 to –0.48 s, sum[t(85)]=–78.2, and pcorr=0.022).
source: In contrast, for the daIns, when baseline BGA was high, choice-related BGA negatively predicts choices (best cluster: –0.74 to –0.48 s, sum[t(85)]=–78.2, and pcorr=0.022).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this statistical finding.

claim: kg was significantly enhanced by vmPFC baseline (t[90] = 3.16 and p=2.10–3).
source: Comparing posterior parameters obtained with high- vs. low-BGA trials (obtained by median split), we found that kg was significantly enhanced by vmPFC baseline (t[90] = 3.16 and p=2.10–3; two-sided, paired, Student's t-test)

claim: Increased vmPFC BGA would lead to overestimating gain prospects, while increased daIns BGA would lead to overestimating loss prospects.
source: This suggests that iEEG baseline fluctuations in these two mood-related regions had opposite effects: increased vmPFC BGA would lead to overestimating gain prospects, while increased daIns BGA would lead to overestimating loss prospects.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this interpretation of the computational modeling results.

claim: The basic assumption of the mood model is that mood is nothing but a weighted sum of positive and negative events (feedbacks received in the quiz task), the more recent having more weight than the more distant in the past.
source: The basic assumption is that mood is nothing but a weighted sum of positive and negative events (here, feedbacks received in the quiz task), the more recent having more weight than the more distant in the past.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes the basic assumption of the mood model.

claim: The mood model postulates that the way feedbacks are perceived are also affected by mood, in the sense that a same feedback is perceived as more positive when we are in a better mood.
source: In addition, the model postulates that the way feedbacks are perceived are also affected by mood, in the sense that a same feedback is perceived as more positive when we are in a better mood.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes this postulate of the mood model.

claim: The mood model was inverted on the basis of mood ratings and compared to a null model, where mood is just drifting with time, without any influence of feedback.
source: The model was inverted on the basis of mood ratings and compared to a null model, where mood is just drifting with time, without any influence of feedback.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes the model comparison approach.

claim: The mood model's evidence was surpassing the null model in about two-thirds of subjects.
source: Even if the mood model was largely winning the Bayesian comparison at the group level, its evidence was surpassing the null model in about two-thirds of subjects, a proportion close to that reported in the previous publication (Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly reports this finding and cites a previous study.

claim: The time scale of mood fluctuations was longer than acute emotional reactions to single stimuli but much shorter than those observed in mood disorders.
source: Thus, the time scale of mood fluctuations was longer than acute emotional reactions to single stimuli but much shorter than those observed in mood disorders.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this characterization of the time scale.

claim: The vmPFC and daIns are implicated in reward learning and punishment learning, respectively.
source: This is consistent with many studies implicating the vmPFC in reward learning and the daIns in punishment learning (Fouragnan et al., 2018; Garrison et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2011; Palminteri and Pessiglione, 2017), including studies using iEEG (Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: The Discussion section cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: The vmPFC and daIns integrate feedbacks over a longer time scale than just the last reward or punishment outcome.
source: What we additionally show here is that the vmPFC and daIns are not just sensitive to the last reward or punishment outcome as in learning paradigms but integrate feedbacks over a longer time scale.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this as a novel finding of the study.

claim: The ventral striatum has been shown to correlate positively with mood level.
source: We note that some expected regions are missing in our list, notably the ventral striatum, which has been shown to correlate positively with mood level (Eldar and Niv, 2015; Rutledge et al., 2014; Young and Nusslock, 2016).
evidence: The Discussion section cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: The ventral striatum could not be investigated in this study because it was not sampled by the electrodes implanted for clinical purposes.
source: This region could not be investigated here because it was simply not sampled by the electrodes implanted for clinical purposes (i.e. for localization of epileptic foci).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this limitation.

claim: An inherent limitation to iEEG is that parts of the brain are less sampled than others, so null results should be considered with caution.
source: More generally, an inherent limitation to iEEG is that parts of the brain are less sampled than others, so null results should be considered with caution, because of huge differences in statistical power across regions.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this limitation of the iEEG method.

claim: Whole-brain analysis using fMRI showed that with this induction procedure, activity in other regions such as the ventral striatum or dorsal anterior cingulate cortex adds nothing to decoding of mood level.
source: Nevertheless, whole-brain analysis using fMRI showed that with this induction procedure, activity in other regions such as the ventral striatum or dorsal anterior cingulate cortex adds nothing to decoding of mood level (Vinckier et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a previous fMRI study supporting this claim.

claim: Higher mood had opposite effects on high-frequency oscillations in the vmPFC and daIns, with increased BGA in the vmPFC but decreased BGA in the daIns.
source: On the contrary, we observed that higher mood had opposite effects on high-frequency oscillations in the two regions, with increased BGA in the vmPFC but decreased BGA in the daIns.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Mood fluctuations were better accounted for by relative high-frequency activity (BGA) in the two opponent regions.
source: Thus, mood fluctuations were better accounted for by relative high-frequency activity (BGA) in the two opponent regions.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: When included in the same model, vmPFC and daIns BGA were both significant predictors of mood level.
source: Indeed, when included in the same model, vmPFC and daIns BGA were both significant predictors of mood level.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Including low-frequency activity in the model did not help predicting mood level.
source: Conversely, including low-frequency activity in the model did not help predicting mood level.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The information carried in low-frequency activity was at best redundant with that of high-frequency activity, whereas the two regions carried at least partly independent information.
source: The information carried in low-frequency activity was therefore at best redundant with that of high-frequency activity, whereas the two regions carried at least partly independent information.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Higher BGA signaled the two extreme tertiles: good mood in the vmPFC and bad mood in the daIns.
source: When analyzing separately bad, neutral, and good mood levels, we found that higher BGA signaled the two extreme tertiles: good mood in the vmPFC and bad mood in the daIns.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The two regions (vmPFC and daIns) were specifically concerned with good and bad mood, explaining why they were not just anti-correlated.
source: This result suggests that the two regions were specifically concerned with good and bad mood, explaining why they were not just anti-correlated, as previously suggested (Kucyi et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation and cites a previous study.

claim: Mood could be bidimensional, meaning that good and bad mood would be better conceived as independent components.
source: Although we used a unidimensional rating going from bad to good mood, it could be that mood is in fact bidimensional, meaning that good and bad mood would be better conceived as independent components (Watson et al., 1988), relying on distinct brain systems.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly suggests this possibility and cites a previous study.

claim: Absence of positive affect or excess of negative affect is considered as two independent criteria for depression in clinical practice.
source: This is in keeping with clinical practice: absence of positive affect or excess of negative affect is considered as two independent criteria for depression.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this clinical practice.

claim: The observation that mood is signaled by distinct brain systems and not different frequency bands all over the brain might be related to the use of positive and negative events to induce mood fluctuations and not direct stimulation of the cortical surface.
source: The observation that mood is signaled by distinct brain systems and not different frequency bands all over the brain as in previous iEEG studies (Bijanzadeh et al., 2013; Kirkby et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2018) might be related to the use of positive and negative events to induce mood fluctuations and not direct stimulation of the cortical surface, which might put constraints on oscillatory activity.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly suggests this explanation and cites previous studies.

claim: The good correspondence with previous fMRI results validates the shared view that BGA represents a time-resolved neural index of local neuronal activity, which typically correlates with both hemodynamic response and local spiking activity.
source: Besides, the good correspondence with previous fMRI results validates the shared view that BGA represents a time-resolved neural index of local neuronal activity, which typically correlates with both hemodynamic response and local spiking activity (Lachaux et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2009; Mukamel et al., 2005; Niessing et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007; Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this validation and cites multiple studies.

claim: The study has confirmed the correspondence between iEEG and fMRI activity every time they compared them during the same behavioral paradigm.
source: We have confirmed this correspondence every time we compared iEEG and fMRI activity during the same behavioral paradigm (Gueguen et al., 2021; Lopez-Persem et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion section cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Choice to accept or reject the challenge was significantly modulated by the three attributes displayed on screen: gain prospect, loss prospect, and difficulty of the challenge.
source: Choice to accept or reject the challenge in our task was significantly modulated by the three attributes displayed on screen: gain prospect (in case of success), loss prospect (in case of failure), and difficulty of the challenge.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: On top of the three attributes, good/bad mood inclined subjects to accept/reject the challenge.
source: Those residuals were significantly impacted by mood level, meaning that on top of the other factors, good/bad mood inclined subjects to accept/reject the challenge.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Higher baseline BGA in the vmPFC/daIns was both predicted by good/bad mood and associated to higher accept/reject rates, relative to predictions of the choice model.
source: The same was true for neural correlates of mood: higher baseline BGA in the vmPFC/daIns was both predicted by good/bad mood and associated to higher accept/reject rates, relative to predictions of the choice model.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Different mood levels might translate into different brain states that predispose subjects to make risky or safe decisions.
source: Thus, different mood levels might translate into different brain states that predispose subjects to make risky or safe decisions (Figure 4).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this conclusion and references a figure.

claim: Higher BGA in the vmPFC/daIns predicted the likelihood of accept/reject choices during decision making.
source: We found some carry-over: higher BGA in the vmPFC/daIns again predicted the likelihood of accept/reject choices.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The link between BGA and choice was lost at the offer onset and retrieved before the behavioral response.
source: This does not mean that the link between BGA and choice was maintained all along; it was actually lost at the offer onset and retrieved before the behavioral response.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this temporal pattern.

claim: The impact of baseline activity in mood-related regions was mediated by the contribution of the same regions (vmPFC and daIns) to the decision-making process.
source: It suggests that the impact of baseline activity in mood-related regions was mediated by the contribution of the same regions (vmPFC and daIns) to the decision-making process.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: The vmPFC and daIns have been implicated in computing the subjective values that are compared to make a choice, with the vmPFC and daIns, respectively, providing positive and negative value signals.
source: These regions have already been implicated in computing the subjective values that are compared to make a choice, with the vmPFC and daIns, respectively, providing positive and negative value signals (Bartra et al., 2013; Pessiglione and Delgado, 2015).
evidence: The Discussion section cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: The relative activity of vmPFC and daIns may provide an impulse to accept or reject an offer, depending on whether the differential is positive or negative.
source: Thus, the relative activity of two regions may provide an impulse to accept or reject an offer, depending on whether the differential is positive or negative.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: High BGA in the vmPFC/daIns was respectively associated to overweighting of gain and loss prospects.
source: We found that high BGA in the vmPFC/daIns was respectively associated to overweighting of gain and loss prospects and not just the constant that captures the global tendency to accept or reject.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Pre-stimulus spiking or hemodynamic activity in the vmPFC predicts how much rewards are liked.

evidence: The Discussion section cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Mood-related neural fluctuations impact the valuation process in a valence-specific way, implemented by functionally opponent brain systems.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that mood-related neural fluctuations impact the valuation process in a valence-specific way, implemented by functionally opponent brain systems.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this conclusion.

source: In fact, those trials can only degrade the correlation with computational variables, such that keeping them ensures that results would be more robust to replication.

claim: At longer time scales, these mechanisms could explain why people take more gambles (or less) after incidental events such as the victory (or defeat) of their favorite sport team.
source: At longer time scales, these mechanisms could explain why people take more gambles (or less) after incidental events such as the victory (or defeat) of their favorite sport team, an effect that might be exacerbated in pathological conditions such as during manic (or depressive) episodes.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly suggests this broader implication.

claim: The impact of mood on choice is a form of generalization, across different sources of reward and punishment, that may be catastrophic in pathological cases.
source: The impact of mood on choice is a form of generalization, across different sources of reward and punishment, that may be catastrophic in pathological cases, leading people to believe that because they experienced positive (or negative) outcome in some part of their life, they are likely to succeed (or fail) in any other.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation.
